The RNG on this game is really criminal, you need a good combo in order to make a good run. You need to keep gambling with stuff and forge, meanwhile you get equips you dont need and will probably just delete them from your inventory, meaning all that gambling was for nothing Sounds like hell, i like it.

First of all the game is kind of fun and feels fresh for arround 10 hours. You can win the game with some effort and rerolling runs and if you are lucky... what brings me to the negatives about the game.... After this time and several unlocks you'll most likely find out the same I did. The games balancing is god awefull. It's so trash tier I have no words. You either have a god run where everything aligns perfectly or you'll be shred into bits every time. Restarting the game 10 times because the passive skills are either game winning or a certain loss with nothing inbetween is terrible. On top of it there are sets in the game that can't win the game if you don't have a godrun without specific bosses in your way. It's pathetic and kind of a beta state instead of an release.

Demo时因为流程较短没暴露出来的问题在正式版完全暴露了出来： 1. 一个非常吃运气的游戏，初期能否拿到强力流派的道具直接决定了你能否通关。 2. 没有局外成长，意味着每一次死亡都需要从头再来。 3. 平衡性不好，一些流派的体验非常差 总结：如果是想玩得爽，建议不要买，纯坐牢 --------------------------------------------------- 补充：打了六个多小时才用初始人物通关，解锁了【用初始人物通关】的成就，一看成就完成率差一点才到60% 就能看出这个游戏在难度设计上的不合理了

Maybe i'm missing something here but the game seems like 100% RNG. If the game wants to deal you a bad hand, you loose. No tactics or strategy will save you. Sure everyone loves loot. But even if you wanted to go for a particular synergy or strategy with your gear you’re completely at the games mercy as to what drops for you. Normally this would be fine in a game where you can move and explore. But this is a linear path with randomly generated difficulty in the monsters you fight. To me it feels like its biggest strength and biggest flaw is its simplicity in game play.

游戏体量不大，20小时左右就能全成就。目前游戏时长50小时，但因为最近一直都是开着游戏看TI，比赛间隔切出来打一把，实际时长大概在30-40小时吧。 整体游戏机制还是挺好玩的，装备套装和怪物机制也能感受到作者是用心设计的，至于这种“设计”玩家喜不喜欢就是另外一回事了。当然我也挺讨厌“亡语”效果，但无法否认这个设计是逼玩家去花心思构筑BD。 如果你的期望是割草类，那这个游戏打到难5确实是很难割草，很看RNG运气因素。但实际上熟悉机制以后不靠运气也能比较稳定通关难5，胜率往低了估计我觉得也至少有七八成以上。比如狗哥这个角色自带一条命，3层给个回满血药水，等于自带3条命，留一大堆药水进boss，哪怕二三技能完全没用，也是有很大希望过的。刚打了一把狗哥就是技能纯没用，套装也不算成型，单靠一个神器鞋子，3国王2仙灵配毒+钝击慢慢磨死了boss。 游戏的策略性体现在两方面，主要部分是背包管理和BD选择，次要部分是优先攻击的目标。后一部分的话，同一套装备打同一队敌人，优先攻击的目标不同可能会导致完全不同的结果。这方面主要是你要对自己的伤害有基本预估，打熟悉了就清楚什么装备优先该先打谁了。 主要讲讲背包管理和BD选择的技巧吧。 1）一般情况不推荐强行玩某个套路，先看技能书发什么技能（相当于天赋），再选择未来BD的方向。每次点开技能书会提前看到下一层技能的选项。当然确实技能之间不太平衡，有的技能明显只能靠特定套路玩。 2）如何贪发育：发育套装主要是3套，村民，盐水，王室。开局找3件村民套，一般不推荐5村民贪发育，除非你有2把稀有村民斧+稀有村民戒指（村民只有斧头和戒指的稀有）。然后找海盗盐水套，找到盐水以后村民就可以退休了，如果2层前期还没找到不推荐强行贪，优先提升战斗力。保持3盐水+另外2件凑个额外套装，如果能凑到5盐水当然是最好。最后王室套的问题，王室套的高运气是能影响普通箱子的稀有度，但前期战斗力偏弱，后期拿到王室套的时候运气其实也没啥用了，定位略尴尬，与其当成发育套装，不然当成后期辅助buff效果（上毒、创伤或者仙灵的恶咒）。最后提一点，高运气只影响普通箱子的稀有度，不影响金箱子（包括盐水给的金箱子）和boss箱子，所以运气和盐水套装不是非常适配。 3）前期过度：一层白字护甲优于闪避，闪避不到四十都没什么作用。比较好用的前期套装主要是暗棘、铁军、奥秘、仙灵，而且这几套都是2件就有套装生效，很适配3村民或者3海盗发育。前两者是高护甲+被动群体伤害，后两者是高魔法群体伤害，但奥秘和仙灵过渡主要是靠武器输出，衣服和首饰的加成都太低前期不推荐。剩下的2件就能生效的套装，军团和浪人只能算勉强能用，但是一个加激昂一个加创伤，都是出伤太慢，一定要用的话军团略强于浪人。林人和隐侠（刺客）就完全不适合过渡，还是那个问题，暴击、闪避、灵敏这些概率属性不到四十可以当成没有。当然这些不是完全绝对的，比如隐侠如果有1技能加暴击，然后前期稀有给个加暴击的，那肯定也还是能用。最后禁巫、玄秘、无面、野兽这些套装都是3件才生效，前期不要想了，刚好来一件高稀有度然后你那个位置上还没有东西的时候可以暂时带一个。 4）中后期BD选择：中后期在背包留什么装备的时候一定要考虑到，并不是所有套装都有紫装橙装的。实际上每个套装都只有2-3件橙装，甚至可能缺紫装。比如林人和隐侠都是只有武器和鞋有橙，奥秘只有法杖和帽子有橙，仙灵是法杖帽子鞋子3件有橙但是首饰最高只到蓝色稀有。有时候你觉得是自己运气不好，一直没见到自己想找的套装的紫装橙装，但你可能不知道，你想找的那个装备实际上根本不存在。这点是游戏做的特别不好的一点，因为大家一般都会默认每个套装的每个位置应该是各个稀有度都有的，但实际上不是，游戏里应该做个套装物品列表出来。同样的，因为大量套装的橙装位置重叠，甚至缺紫装，实际上是很难互相配合的，比如林人和隐侠，2个橙装位置完全重叠，除非你打狗哥3技能给了个1件3星装备算2件，不然后期没法两套一起成型。 然后具体的BD选择上，有很多套装只推荐激活一层效果，多了收益很低。还是比如林人和游侠，4件6件和2件没有太大本质提升，与其凑到6，不如拿另外一套。同样的，野兽3件30%和5件50%群伤没有特别大提升。所以适合主打的，推荐还是仙灵、奥秘、无面、浪人、铁军、暗棘，其他套装根据你的主打可以做辅助，比如主仙灵+副林人/浪人/王室/奥秘（副隐侠需要玩暗影角色然后1技能给魔法暴击，因为魔法原本不吃暴击），比如主无面+副隐侠/野兽，比如主奥秘+副仙灵（主奥秘爆发高但生存力太弱，副仙灵推荐衣服和鞋加闪避提高生存），比如主浪人+副王室等等。最后就是主铁军和暗棘如果没有特别好的角色3技能支持，打过3层没问题但是最终boss会打不过（相当于爬塔打不过心脏），所以打难5要准备好替代方案。 最后，如果你到3层中间已经感觉这把最终很难凑出套装了，或者你的角色3技能给的不是特别适配，神器给的也不行，那就要考虑最终boss的替代方案了。注意，以下仅说的是未成型的情况，你已经成型了而且技能也好那就没必要考虑这些。 一般来说因为boss机制会持续给你上毒上创伤上虚弱，如果你的输出没法在debuff叠高之前打死boss的话，那就只能考虑想办法控制住boss然后慢慢磨死。因为虚弱的存在，想磨死靠物理是很难的，推荐是苟毒和魔法，这俩不吃虚弱。然后生存方面要么把闪避拉到80%以上，要么想办法找多段攻击+钝击控制住boss，这样尽量只吃到毒的伤害不会被boss打。算好血量（注意毒伤也吃创伤加成），前面先靠血药顶，然后顶不住毒伤了就磕一个消除debuff的回血丹，另外狗哥因为多一条命所以打最终boss还是挺稳的。提供毒和钝击的方面，禁巫的戒指，王室的匕首，玄秘的戒指和法杖，这些都可以成为最终没有办法的时候的办法。 = 所以最终来看，这个游戏其实是存在的决策和BD成分的，也需要考验玩家对于数值和游戏机制的理解，并非很多人认为的纯看运气。不过客观上来讲，一旦达到这个阶段，这游戏也就变得没什么意思了。游戏体量摆在那里，框架也就这么大，最多也就调整下技能树，很难说再增加更多的游戏时长。 话是这么说，最近看TI等比赛的时间也没啥其他新游戏可以打发时间的了（打丝之歌需要的专注度和看比赛冲突了不考虑），大概还是会在间隙时不时开几把的……
感觉作者对于装备套装设计有缺点，不够平衡，这里推荐一下套装选择攻略，无脑选林人就行了，再搭配一下军团或者其他有盾牌，要是有吸血就可以杀遍天下无敌手了，总得来说作者不会设计，除了林人以外其他套装都很难打通关，就军团那点护甲根本比不了一点躲闪和灵敏

Had fun the first run I did, but then after that I started to see how little depth there is to this game. For a game based on loot and with loot in the title, you would think the loot would actually be interesting. Spoiler alert, it is not. The whole loot system basically comes down to increasing whatever stat you are basing your build around, and that's about it. As for combat strategy, there isn't much outside of kill the guy who does the most dmg first, with few exceptions.

Overlooting, developed and published by Posing Possums, is a pixel-art roguelite that manages to carve a distinct identity in a crowded genre by doing something deceptively clever: it turns inventory management—a mechanic usually taken for granted—into the beating heart of its gameplay loop. It’s not just about finding loot; it’s about making hard decisions with it, understanding synergies, and learning when to hoard and when to cut your losses. The result is a game that feels familiar in its structure but novel in its execution, offering a refreshingly strategic twist for fans of roguelike dungeon-crawlers. You begin each run by selecting one of three distinct characters, each with their own passive abilities and starting bonuses. This initial choice already sets the tone for your playthrough, as each hero leans into different archetypes—whether it’s Maximilian’s straightforward power, Liz’s luck-based modifiers, or the more complex traits of The Shadow. From there, you dive into a world split into themed regions filled with enemies, chests, random events, and bosses. What’s compelling here isn’t just the combat encounters themselves—which are functional but not overly complex—but how every decision you make outside of battle impacts your ability to survive the next one. The flow of battle, loot, and management forms a seamless cycle that becomes more addictive the more you play. Loot in Overlooting is everything. Not just a reward, but a dynamic system that shapes your build and your fate. Each item you find belongs to a gear set, and assembling sets provides powerful bonuses—some defensive, some offensive, and others offering utility or economic advantages. But with limited inventory space, you constantly have to weigh immediate benefit against potential synergy. Should you keep a half-finished set in the hope that you’ll find the missing piece, or ditch it for something that offers an instant stat boost? These dilemmas occur frequently and are where the game shines brightest. The inventory screen becomes your planning board, and every slot matters. In that sense, the game forces you to think several steps ahead in a way that many roguelites don’t. What keeps each run fresh is the procedurally generated skill tree system. Unlike many games where your build grows along the same predictable path, Overlooting reshuffles your upgrade options every time. This forces you to constantly re-strategize and adapt your loot and combat style to what the skill tree offers. It also means that no two runs play out exactly the same, which gives the game significant replay value. Combined with the gradually unlocking corruption system—essentially a difficulty modifier that makes enemies tougher but increases rewards—each new run feels like a meaningful step forward, not just a repetition of the last. The visual style is pixelated but polished, with a clean presentation that prioritizes clarity and information over flashy effects. This works well for the kind of game Overlooting is—one that relies on players quickly parsing item stats, recognizing set icons, and scanning for synergy potential. Enemy designs are varied enough to keep things visually interesting, and while animations are minimal, they’re snappy and readable. The soundtrack and audio design are modest but effective, supporting the mood without drawing too much attention. It’s clear that the developers focused their efforts where it matters most: on tight systems and gameplay flow. Still, Overlooting isn’t without its rough patches. RNG, for instance, plays a major role—sometimes perhaps too much. A few unlucky loot drops or an uncooperative skill tree can handicap your run early, making some losses feel more like the fault of the game than the player. While this is a common issue in roguelites, the game could benefit from more mechanisms to mitigate bad luck, such as more consistent ways to reroll skills or salvage gear. There are also moments where combat becomes a bit repetitive, particularly in the mid-game, where enemy variety thins out before bosses pick things up again. Additionally, some of the tooltips and item descriptions lack clarity, which can be frustrating when trying to make split-second inventory decisions. What Overlooting gets right, though, far outweighs its flaws. It takes the tried-and-true roguelite format and makes it feel tactical in a way that’s rarely explored. The game rewards careful thought, forward planning, and experimentation, not just fast reflexes or meta knowledge. It encourages you to play the long game, to think like a dungeon-crawling accountant juggling a bag of cursed artifacts, and it pulls that off in a way that’s both satisfying and replayable. For players who find joy in organizing their inventory, optimizing builds on the fly, and adapting to procedural chaos, this is a game that will likely hook you quickly and keep you coming back. In the end, Overlooting is a smart, well-crafted roguelite that understands the appeal of the genre but isn’t afraid to subvert expectations. It’s challenging without being punishing, strategic without being slow, and chaotic without losing control. If you're looking for something that feels both accessible and deep, where loot isn't just the end goal but the core mechanic, Overlooting is more than worth your time. It may fly under the radar for some, but for fans of clever game design and satisfying systems, this one’s a gem. Rating: 8/10

Recommended for the meta progression (unlocking characters and the 5 difficulty increases) which takes about 10 hours. Not recommended for achievements (takes 30-50 more hours). The game has all the hallmarks of a very repeatable game. Pick a character (of 3). Finish 3 floors, each with about 45 rooms ( [ monster room x 3, event room ] x 10 + a boss). Done. Pixel art is well done, npc, boss and item variety exists, lots of set bonuses and character talents. So why "Not recommended"? Unlocking the Set Achievements (15 excluding Exotics) was not fun for me. * Floor normal fights are not randomized * Floor events are not randomized * Floors are too long * Limited influence over drops (Luck and Villager Set) [h2]My achievement grinding solution[/h2] * Pick The Shadow" (to maximize chance of Set drops) * Pick Corruption 0 * Run the first 10 or so fights for Villager 3 and end the first floor with Darkthorn 2 (life steal purple whip can carry you) * Reset boss fight "Pick 2 Set Bonuses" event due to the fact the game is unseeded and you can alt-f4 I didn't start with this strategy, I earned a few achievements organically. But about half way through the list of achievements I was done, I had memorized the maps, died to the expected monster packs and it wasn't fun playing through the same 40-50% of the game hoping to explore the Set the achievement was designed around. If you think I am wrong? You do you. But play endless too. Did you quit, or did the fights beat you? [h2]What I would change[/h2] * Seed fights/chests (quitting/reloading should result in same dice roll/outcomes) * Add/move 3 sets to specific characters * Quality of Life: Make all sets show up on your character panel (excluding mytics) from the start. This means a new player can hover their mouse over Hex 0 and see the tooltip. Players can use this when comparing items in that state before they have memorized everything. * Shrink floors by 35% ( monster x3, event) x 7 + boss (45 down to 29), only possible if you have more control over finishing sets * Make events Random. The pool of events should be (forge, potions, upgrade, dummy) and about 10-15 more (e.g. an event that sacrifices an item for you to gain +1 innate from a set on that item). The community forums are littered with ideas but fundamentally they should allow the player some control over set acquisition. * Consider a pity* system on loot drops. * Split the NPCS on a floor into groups (e.g. floor 1 could be Slimes, Imps and Insects). Example: Floor 1 "slime boss", you face Green slimes, Splitter Slimes (slimes which when killed spawn more slimes), Thorny Slimes, Explosive Slimes (damage is split between player and remaining monsters), Iron Slimes (hitting them gives you 1 barrier but they take only 1 damage per hit), Poisonous Slimes, etc. Just color swap them. The key is to add a bit of diversity across game play. [h2]Pity System[/h2] Consider a quest "Collect 5 rat ears from rats". You add a Rat to the game world, give them a drop table of an ear and set its drop rate of 5%. How long will it take players to get 5 rat ears? Answer, it could be infinite. That is the nature of probabilities. Enter 2004's World of Warcraft. Quest Designer adds an integer, Pity P of 5. Players in their quest log have a hidden number N which has a value between 0 and P. Kill a rat? Increase N by 1. If N == P, you get an Ear and N is reset to 0. You pitied". Same question: How long will it take players to get 5 rat ears? Answer: No more than 25 rats need to die. This small change (2 integers) changed the gameplay landscape. Games do probability by calling a function such as get_random() which returns a value between 0 and 1 (0% and 100%). Write a new get_random_with_probilty(N,P) which returns (probability, used_pity). You pass in N and P update N in the database based on used_pity (resetting if true, or increasing by 1 if not). How to use in Overlooting to "bias" loot. Consider P' = 15 (number of sets) - (equipped # from set), minimum 1. Set Call get_random_with_pity(N,P') for each equipped set. If the resulting probability is 1.0 "that player should get a set". Look at the loot that is available to the player for their given floor/stage/luck. Is there an item with this set? If set "Give it as an option and reset N". Reset the N's for the other Sets in the loot presented to the player. This may gametest poorly, as I arbitrarily chose 15 and 3*(equipped set items). But we're talking a few integers in the code to cause a multitude of biasing of loot. Multiple Pities can be combined (i.e. have multiple N's be reset as the result of one success) and you end up with a hearthstone pack (i.e. Legendary guarenteed after 40 packs (i.e. 200 cards), with individual probability of 0.25%, which when it succeeds resets Epic, Rare pities as well). The biggest issue with the game is that it is too dependant on RNG. Unlike other roguelikes where even when you get screwed by RNG there's at least a bit of hope of making it through skill alone, in this game it's ALL RNG. The random drops are all you really have, and outside from some small moments there's really no way to control how your run will go. Sometimes you won't get a good weapon for your build for ages, and other times the boss of the area is specifically designed to counter your build. If you try to go for achievements prepare yourself to reset a hundred times until you finally get a good run going. I think I like the idea of the game (Hell, I even did all the achievements) but by the end it became such an awful grind, especially when trying to get some of the weaker combos. And it sucks that there's no good strategy other than praying that you get good items early.

[h2][i]Overlooting[/i] is a fun roguelike missing some spice.[/h2] I'd appreciate the addition of more characters, a bigger loot pool, act variation (ideally with branching), and more opportunity to select skill points, as three is a very small number to stop at. This is also a game I imagine mods would add a lot to, particularly since it's an offline, single-player PvE experience, without any leaderboards. Alas, [i]there is no mod support,[/i] which is a shame, Speaking of leaderboards: Now that endless mode has been released, I think leaderboards would actually be pretty neat. There could be one for total areas, one for amount of loops, and then another for speed runs, all broken down by character. Speaking of: I'd be remiss not to briefly speak on the imbalance between the three characters. [b]Maximilian the dog[/b] is way too good and nearly incapable of dying outside of endless mode. [u]I'd rank his passives and skills 7 — 10 out of 10.[/u] [b]Liz the cat[/b] feels like a weaker version of Maximilian, and her skills focus too heavily on potions. [u]I'd rank her passives and skills 3 — 8 out of 10.[/u] [b]The Shadow[/b] feels incredibly punishing to play and only ever pushes far with very specific builds. [u]I'd rank its passives and skills -5 — 5 out of 10.[/u] Yes, that is to say NEGATIVE 5 to positive 5. Ideally, all of the above would be addressed, since I can't stress enough how suboptimal it feels to play as anything other than Maximilian. This choice feels like picking between three difficulties [i]—tutorial, medium, and nightmare—[/i] when character choice should boil down to gameplay, build variety, or some other fun-based factor instead. Where's the fun in stacking potions? Why are half of The Shadow's skills so bad that they feel like a negative? Without regen or an absurd amount of life steal, The Shadow can't even rely on its strongest skills, as they'll kill it before the end of the first act. If combat were a little more engaging (the only strategy is what set pieces to equip and what order to mow enemies down in), perhaps by means of even just a handful of usable skills, less people would think the game is boring. As much as I'd view the above as an added bonus, I don't really think it's boring at all. Inventory management is the core of the game, which works out pretty well. The game's name is [i]'Overlooting,'[/i] after all. I once beat a run where I had equipped three or four unique, red quality items (mythics), with their single-piece set bonus, including [i]'speedster'[/i] (think [i]Windfury[/i] from [i]WoW[/i]), and [b]I was having a blast watching my character become exponentially stronger and just absolutely shredding through mobs.[/b] So many one-shots! Ultimately, this game is either going to click with a player or not, and I'd say that largely depends on if one is looking for good systems (present) or engaging combat (absent). Something I love about [i]Overlooting[/i] is the fact that hopping on and off the game is seamless, each area takes only a few seconds to get through, and the player is in complete control over how much time he/she wants to invest. I believe one can save at any point (a feature I've only had to use once in 13 hours of play), so if a run is turning out better than expected and something comes up, no worries. That being said, sitting down for several hours and experiencing the game with a [i]"one more run"[/i] mindset is also very common. [b]Easy to pick up, easy to put down, and yet somehow strangely addicting,[/b] in spite of the negatives outlined above, which really more so serve as a personal wish list to make the game even better. [i]Overlooting[/i] has all the makings of a great roguelike, but needs just a couple of extra minutes in the oven. I'd implore the devs to add more content. The players will thank you, and the game will sell even better. As it stands right now, the game is good for what it is, but I'd like to see it become great. Regardless, I will continue revisiting it, since I've been enjoying my time. EDIT: I've been playing this game a lot more, and now I really want to see enchantments and/or socketable gems for even deeper customization.

Got this one through Humble Bundle and I hate to say but there isn't much to write home about it. It seems to be going primarily for an auto-battler style synergy system (think Teamfight Tactics, Super Auto Pets or Dota Underlords) but attached to a relatively bare-bones battle system: Once you've got a decent bit of momentum you really don't have to think about the fights, it's all about optimizing your build with what you get. While there is no real way to push your build in any given direction, the game showers you with enough loot over the course of a run that you really don't feel it. On to the nitty-gritty, though, I do think the potions being part of the same inventory as the loot causes more problems than it helps. Even in the trailer you can see a few scenes where the character's inventory is a good 50% potions, and the encounters aren't necessarily challenging enough to justify it. If you need to use a potion to get through an encounter then you're probably not on a winning run. The randomization also isn't helping when it comes down to character talent selection: You can't see what talents you're going to have access to until you've unlocked the first one, and they are assigned in random sets of 3... so you can go into a run hoping to use X set (of which there are achievements for beating the game with a set maxed out) so you might be setting off hoping to build around magic damage, only for your characters talent screen to offer no magic synergy this time around. Same goes for the end-of-map free set bonuses: While they aren't necessary to complete a specific build, they open up a lot more room for tooling around with your items and it's a real downer when you can't get one in the set you were looking for. Overall, it's alright for a bit of light roguelike entertainment, but it doesn't particularly stand out in the genre in any meaningful way. I'd say wait for a sale.

This was ok at first but it gets insanely repetitive with little to no metaprogression. I thought I'd grind this out for the achievements but I just can't. Runs take way too long, build synergies are few and far in between, and the enemy variety is honestly just embarrassing. Feels more like a cool tech demo than an actual finished game, with only 3 characters, a handful of gear sets and like maybe a dozen enemies, you've seen everything the game has to offer in the first 2 hours, after that it's just grinding for achievements, that's it, nothing left to unlock, nothing left to discover. Maybe a choose-your-own-path map would have made this better, but in Overlooting, you just automatically move from one area to the next. Overall it doesn't make for very engaging gameplay imo and the couple hours I wasted thinking I could 100% this one in a couple days has left a sour taste in my mouth. If you can get it for dirt cheap, sure pick it up, but I would never pay full price for this when there's similar games out there that are infinitely better than this.
